newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters agree to end strike.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters agree to end strike.

text.p: United Parcel Service, the world's largest parcel delivery company, settled with workers on Tuesday after a 15-day strike that has cost UPS $650 million and crippled many small U.S. businesses.

At picket lines near UPS headquarters in Atlanta, thousands of Teamster union members cheered the tentative settlement of the biggest walkout in at least 21 years, widely seen as a victory for U.S. organized labor.

After almost 90 hours of negotiations under the auspices of Labor Secretary Alexis Herman in Washington, Teamsters President Ron Carey said the union had won sweeping concessions from UPS, a giant blue-chip corporation with annual revenues of $22.4 billion.

The company will convert 10,000 part-time jobs into full-time jobs over the five years of a new contract and hourly wage rates will rise by up to about 36 percent over the same period, Carey told a news conference.
The bad news for the union was that UPS threatened job cuts, citing the loss of business from the strike.
"Unfortunately, 5 percent of our business is susceptible to being lost. ... We're predicting 15,000 (jobs) will not be necessary," UPS spokesman Ken Sternad told Cable News Network.
"We're hoping it (the job losses) will be less than that," UPS Chairman James Kelly told a news conference later.

Carey said the 185,000 striking workers, who received $55 a week in union strike benefits, could go back to work as early as Wednesday. Union officials said local union leaders would meet in Washington later Tuesday to vote on the deal.
The union leader, who had staked his reputation on the outcome of the strike, hailed the result as a turning point for a union movement that has lost much of its old power.

"This strike marks a new era. American workers have shown that ... we (can) stand up to corporate greed. This victory shows that American workers are on the move again. ... This is the direction corporate America ought to be taking," he said.
Opinion polls showed the UPS strikers had won the battle for the sympathy of most Americans, especially when they rejected the corporate trend toward depending on cheaper part-time workers.
Liberals said the dispute showed it was time to redress the balance between U.S. workers and the big companies that have benefited most from recent economic growth.
Labor Secretary Herman, while declining to say who she thought had won the strike, said the settlement could set a standard for other collective bargaining agreements.

"This agreement certainly has taken historic steps ... and I think it becomes a model for other companies today as we look at the question not only of good wages but also health benefits and retirement security for workers," she said.
The UPS workers pension fund was a key part of the dispute. UPS management had hoped to replace a Teamsters multi-employer plan with a company-controlled plan.
Carey said the union had its way on the pension fund and won generous new benefits. He said a retiring 30-year worker would get monthly benefits of $3,000 or more.
He said the agreement would phase out over six months the use of subcontractors, except during holiday peak periods, giving the jobs instead to UPS workers.
Full-time workers gain $3.10 an hour over five years, while part-timers gain $4.10 over the same period, he said.
Top-rate full-time employees will eventually receive $23 an hour, while top-rate part-timers will move up to about $15 from $11 an hour, he said.
And Carey said if the company wants to raise the package weight limit again, it must negotiate again with the union.
President Bill Clinton patted both sides on the back in an early-morning statement read to reporters in Edgartown, Mass., on Martha's Vineyard, where he was on vacation.
"Today's agreement represents their hard work and determination to reconcile their differences for the good of the company, its employees and the customers they serve," Clinton said.

"The issues that were at the heart of their negotiations are important to our nation's economic strength, and to all Americans." Asked during a walk what he thought of the outcome, Clinton flashed a thumbs-up sign to reporters.

The separate union representing UPS pilots, who refused to work during the Teamsters strike, welcomed the agreement and said it had asked to meet with UPS officials to draw up a return-to-work plan once the Teamsters strike officially ends.
